title: The Last Confession Anew
premise: Estate lawyer Beatrix Yarrow is summoned to probate the will of Marguerite Voss, a woman who vanished five years ago and was declared legally dead — yet the will bears a date after her disappearance. When Beatrix finds Marguerite's diary in the estate's locked study, its entries continue past the disappearance, written in a hand that shifts from confident to desperate to coldly triumphant. As Beatrix and the missing woman's estranged nephew, Daniel Voss, decode the diary, they realize it documents not one death but a slow inheritance scheme built on forged deaths and coerced confessions, orchestrated by someone who has been reading the police file all along. At the anniversary dinner held each year in Marguerite's memory, Beatrix springs her trap: she reads the will aloud with an altered clause that forces the killer — the town's beloved coroner, who faked his own daughter's death to inherit for her — to confess publicly. The diary's final entry, written by Marguerite before her real murder, names him; Beatrix survives the attempt on her life, the estate passes to a scholarship fund, and the town must live with what its filing cabinets kept quiet.
about_author: Ivo Galloway is the pen name of a former small-town court clerk who spent a decade watching wills, deeds, and case files decide what people were allowed to remember. They write mysteries about paper trails and the people who learn too much from them.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Beatrix Yarrow opens the Voss probate file and finds a will dated eleven days after Marguerite Voss disappeared — a legal impossibility she should refuse but doesn't. Her POV establishes her habit of alphabetizing uncomfortable truths. Emotional beat: professional curiosity curdling into dread as she notices the witness signature belongs to a man officially dead since 2019.

chapters.title: Five Years of Flowers
chapters.summary: Beatrix visits Hollow Creek's memorial garden where the town still leaves flowers for Marguerite, interviewing mourners whose grief feels rehearsed. POV alternates with Daniel Voss arriving in town, hostile toward an aunt he never knew. Emotional beat: the uncanny perfection of collective mourning — everyone remembers her fondly, no one remembers her last week.

chapters.title: The Locked Study
chapters.summary: Executing the estate inventory, Beatrix breaks protocol and opens the study sealed since the disappearance, finding the diary hidden inside a hollowed-out Blackstone's Criminal Law. Daniel catches her there. Emotional beat: trespass and complicity — two strangers choosing secrecy together over procedure.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: The diary continues past March 4th, the date Marguerite vanished, in handwriting that deteriorates then hardens into something controlled. Beatrix cross-references dates against the police file she helped archive. Emotional beat: vertigo — the document she trusts most is lying, or the town is.

chapters.title: The Coroner's Kindness
chapters.summary: Dr. Edwin Marsh, the coroner who signed off on Marguerite's presumed death, offers Beatrix warm, unsolicited help navigating the case history — help so precise it unsettles her. His POV briefly shows him reviewing her probate filings at night. Emotional beat: charm as threat; kindness that knows too much.

chapters.title: Daniel's Inheritance of Shame
chapters.summary: Daniel reveals why he stayed away: Marguerite cut off his father years ago after an accusation the family buried. He and Beatrix compare the diary against old letters. Emotional beat: inherited guilt — discovering your family may have been both victim and accomplice.

chapters.title: Alphabetized Secrets
chapters.summary: Beatrix returns to her office archives and reconstructs five years of Voss-adjacent paperwork: property transfers, a second will draft, insurance claims signed by a dead man. Someone has been checking these files out under false names. Emotional beat: the horror of realizing the bureaucracy itself was weaponized.

chapters.title: What the River Kept
chapters.summary: A fisherman finds Marguerite's original locket upstream; inside, a microfilm negative of a confession naming three signatories. Beatrix recognizes one name: Marsh. Daniel wants to go to police; Beatrix warns the file leaks. Emotional beat: proof in hand, safety slipping away.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Committee
chapters.summary: The town's annual dinner for Marguerite approaches, chaired by Marsh himself. Beatrix accepts an invitation to read the will publicly — a decision Daniel calls suicide. Emotional beat: turning fear into strategy; the trap begins forming.

chapters.title: A Forged Hand
chapters.summary: Handwriting analysis confirms the post-disappearance diary entries are imitations — but imitations made from life, by someone who watched Marguerite write. Beatrix realizes the killer kept her captive, alive, dictating her own fiction. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into fury.

chapters.title: The Second Grave
chapters.summary: Following survey discrepancies in the estate deed, Beatrix and Daniel find an unmarked grave on Voss land containing the 'dead' witness, Harold Finch — killed once on paper, twice in fact. Emotional beat: the price of survival paid by the small players while architects walk free.

chapters.title: Marsh's File
chapters.summary: Beatrix breaks into the coroner's office and finds his private copy of the investigation — annotated, corrected, better than the police version, including notes on her own movements. She photographs pages and replaces everything exactly. Emotional beat: hunter becoming hunted; the intimacy of being studied.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Last Week
chapters.summary: Decoding marginalia, they reconstruct Marguerite's final days: she discovered Marsh had falsified his daughter's death to trigger inheritances, and he kept her writing the diary to build his alibi. Emotional beat: the victim regains her voice through the record her killer thought he controlled.

chapters.title: Threats in Triplicate
chapters.summary: Beatrix receives a formal letter citing conflicts of interest demanding she withdraw from probate — legally flawless, personally menacing. Her clerk resigns out of fear. Emotional beat: isolation; the machinery of respectability closing around her.

chapters.title: The Daughter Who Died Twice
chapters.summary: They locate Claire Marsh, alive under a new name two counties over, living well on laundered inheritance money. She agrees to talk only if Beatrix guarantees her father never learns she did. Emotional beat: complicity of the spared — survival bought with silence.

chapters.title: Claire's Testimony
chapters.summary: Claire describes the scheme: staged deaths, coerced confessions, her father's meticulous files. But she refuses to testify, and her account alone proves nothing. Daniel proposes using the anniversary dinner, where tradition demands the will be read. Emotional beat: despair converting into audacity.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for a Trap
chapters.summary: Beatrix drafts a doctored reading of the will inserting a clause voiding all transfers if any beneficiary procured a death certificate — knowing only the killer will understand its target. She rehearses while Marsh watches her office windows. Emotional beat: calm performance over terror.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Marsh confronts Beatrix at her office, offering her partnership in the estate's quiet dissolution — then, refused, promising the dinner will be her last public appearance. Daniel hides the microfilm and diary copies. Emotional beat: the point of no return, chosen deliberately.

chapters.title: Anniversary Dinner
chapters.summary: Before the assembled town, Beatrix reads the altered clause. Marsh, certain the diary survives, moves to silence her mid-sentence; Daniel triggers the prearranged signal and state investigators — tipped with the photographed file — take him down as he lunges. Emotional beat: climax as public unmasking; secrets read aloud become weapons.

chapters.title: Confession, Recorded
chapters.summary: In custody, confronted with the diary's final authentic entry naming him, Marsh confesses with bureaucratic precision, correcting the investigators' timeline out of habit. Marguerite's remains are found where his annotations always pointed. Emotional beat: the monster defeated by his own love of accurate records.

chapters.title: Probate Closed
chapters.summary: Beatrix executes the true will: the estate funds a legal aid clinic for families of the disappeared. Claire testifies voluntarily now; Daniel stays in town, restoring the study. Emotional beat: inheritance redefined — what we leave behind versus what we bury.

chapters.title: A New Filing System
chapters.summary: One year later, Beatrix donates the Voss case file to the town archive, unsealed, and burns her own private copies. Walking past the memorial garden, she finally lets herself grieve a woman she knew only on paper. Emotional beat: resolution — the price of survival acknowledged, the alphabet of secrets finally opened.
